title: What Battle Cards is now
subtitle: A kid who took things apart, four exits, a tech company that became an agency, and an AI lab that rolls up creative studios. Read this first.

content.text: People sometimes ask what ShopOS actually is. The honest answer is that it has been a few different things. Each one made sense at the time. Each one taught us why the next one had to exist.
So this is the story, told the way I would tell it over coffee. Eight short chapters. Then what Battle Cards is, and why you might want to read it.
Chapter one: a kid who took things apart
I liked taking things apart before I liked building them. That habit turned into startups. I sold my first one while I was still in college.

Then I kept going, mostly in deep tech: augmented reality, spatial computing, then AI. Along the way came more than fifteen patents and four exits. Scapic went to Flipkart. Cope.Studio went to Polygon. Reality Tools went to MotionPage. Dehidden went to Layer-E.
Battle Cards started in 2020, in the quiet stretch after Scapic. I wanted to write down the tactical lessons nobody hands you. Small enough to screenshot. Built to be used.
Chapter two: then came ShopOS
ShopOS started as an AI-powered commerce operating system for D2C and Shopify brands. Brands plugged in. We built software to help them sell.
The premise was simple. Brands spend a fortune on catalog, creative and ads, and most of it is manual. If software could do more of it, brands could grow faster.
Chapter three: a tech company, with lots of buttons
So we did what tech companies do. We shipped features. Catalog tools. A feed of daily ideas. Sloosh, our generative media engine. Brand memory. Workflows.
Every feature had a button. Brands liked the buttons. But they kept asking us for the same thing: could you just do it for us?
That question kept coming back. It turned out to be the most important thing anyone told us.
Chapter four: then Claude ate the software
Then the models got good. Really good. Claude, and agents like it, started doing the clicking.
Dashboards, forms, buttons and reports used to be the product. Now an agent can drive all of them. The software layer got thin, fast.

That changed what brands were buying. They never cared which tool made the ad. They cared whether the ad worked. Once agents could run the tools, the tools stopped being the point. The work was the point.
Chapter five: so we became an agency
If the work is the point, someone has to own it. So we became an agency, a full-service one that owns the outcome.
Our performance arm came in when we acquired Crafeed. Our promise to brands became four words: outcomes over outputs. A brand should not pay for forty files. It should pay for the number moving.
Chapter six: agencies run on creative people
Then we learned the oldest lesson in the agency business. Agencies run on people. Specifically, creative people with taste.

AI can make two hundred options before lunch. A human with taste keeps three. That human is the scarce part. Photographers, film makers, writers, designers, editors, performance nerds. You cannot prompt your way to them.
So the question changed again. Not "how do we build more software?" but "how do we work with the best creative people in the world?"
Chapter seven: so we started rolling up studios
The best creative people already have homes. They run studios. Each studio is great at one craft.

So ShopOS became the AI lab that acquires and accelerates creative studios. Founders keep running them. We give them jetpacks: one shared memory of every brand, our generative media engine, and the research team that keeps it all sharp.
The studios are the teams that take the field. The lab is the one underneath them. Every brand gets better the more it works with us, because everything we learn compounds.
That is also why I care so much about slop. The internet is about to fill up with work that has no taste in it. We are betting that taste, written down and run at the speed of software, wins.
Chapter eight: and Battle Cards is the playground
Which brings us back to Battle Cards.

Battle cards are tactical cards and screenshot-sized essays. I hand them to my team. I use them to get better myself. Every card has three parts: what the idea is, why it holds up, and how to use it this week.

Around the cards, this is my playground. It is where I try to build the most audacious crossroads between the creative world and the technology world, and see what comes out. Some of it is long essays. Some of it is live experiments where we hand a new model a real job and watch.
